name: INA128UA_2K5
title: INA128, INA129: precision low-power instrumentation amplifiers, gain 1 to 10000, SOIC-8 and PDIP-8
summary: A three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier whose gain, from 1 to 10000, is set by one resistor across pins 1 and 8. The INA128 uses G = 1 + 50 kΩ/RG and the INA129 G = 1 + 49.4 kΩ/RG. A current-feedback input stage keeps bandwidth at 200 kHz at G = 100 while the supply current is 700 µA; offset is 50 µV max, drift 0.5 µV/°C max and CMR at least 120 dB at G = 100 for P and U parts, and the inputs survive ±40 V. It runs from ±2.25 V to ±18 V and is specified from –40 °C to +85 °C; the die comes from two fabrication flows (CSO: SHE, CSO: FRE) with some separate figures.

notes: INA128 parts use the gain equation G = 1 + 50 kΩ / RG; INA129 parts use G = 1 + 49.4 kΩ / RG. Otherwise the two are specified alike.

P is the 8-pin PDIP and U the 8-pin SOIC. Parts without a trailing A (P, U) carry the tighter offset, drift, gain error, CMRR and bias-current limits of the electrical table; PA and UA parts carry the wider ones.

SOIC parts may carry die from either fabrication flow (CSO: SHE or CSO: FRE); PDIP parts carry CSO: SHE die.

circuits.title: Basic connections
circuits.description: The minimum hookup on split supplies. The input pair goes to VIN+ and VIN–, a single resistor across pins 1 and 8 sets the gain (from the gain resistor table), each supply pin has a 0.1 µF capacitor to ground, and the output is taken from VO into the load with REF tied to the reference voltage, normally ground. VO = G · (VIN+ – VIN–) + VREF.

parts.note: sets the gain: G = 1 + 50 kΩ / RG

notes: For the INA129 the gain is G = 1 + 49.4 kΩ / RG.
Grounding REF is the usual case; about 8 Ω in series with REF lowers CMR to roughly 80 dB at G = 1.

circuits.title: Optional trimming of output offset voltage
circuits.description: Output offset adjustment through REF. Two 100 µA sinks and sources from a REF200 drive a pair of 100 Ω resistors whose middle is grounded, giving about ±10 mV across a 10 kΩ potentiometer. An OPA177 follower buffers the wiper into REF, so REF sees a low impedance and CMR is kept. The adjustment range at the output is ±10 mV.

circuits.title: Bridge amplifier
circuits.description: A 300 Ω resistive bridge excited from +5 V. Its two midpoints, each near 2.5 V and moving by ±ΔV, feed the inputs, and RG sets the gain; REF is grounded, so the output is G times the bridge imbalance.

parts.note: sets the gain: G = 1 + 50 kΩ / RG

notes: VIN+ sits at 2.5 V + ΔV and VIN– at 2.5 V – ΔV.
Supplies are not drawn.

circuits.title: AC-coupled instrumentation amplifier
circuits.description: DC is removed from the output by feedback into REF. An OPA130 integrator (R1 = 1 MΩ into its inverting input, C1 = 0.1 µF from there to its output, non-inverting input grounded) senses VO and drives REF so the output's DC level is held at zero. The result is a high-pass response with f–3dB = 1 / (2π R1 C1) = 1.59 Hz.

circuits.title: Thermocouple amplifier with RTD cold-junction compensation
circuits.description: A type K thermocouple read differentially, with cold-junction compensation from a Pt100 RTD on the same isothermal block as the copper connections. A REF102 makes +10 V; R1 feeds the thermocouple's + lead and R3 (100 Ω, the Pt100's resistance at 0 °C) to ground, while R2 feeds the Pt100 to ground. The two nodes go to VIN+ (Pt100 side) and, through the thermocouple, VIN–; as the block warms, the Pt100 node rises to cancel the cold-junction voltage. R1 and R2 are chosen by thermocouple type from the table; REF is grounded.

circuits.title: Differential voltage to current converter
circuits.description: The output drives a load through R1, and a follower A1 copies the load-side voltage of R1 back onto REF. The voltage across R1 is then G · VIN, so the load current is IO = (VIN / R1) · G. A1's input bias current is the error term; the table lists it for four op amps.

circuits.title: ECG amplifier with right-leg drive
circuits.description: A G = 10 ECG front end. The LA and RA electrode leads run in a shielded cable to VIN+ and VIN–, and RG = 5.6 kΩ is split into two 2.8 kΩ halves whose junction carries the input common-mode voltage VG. One half of an OPA2131 buffers VG onto the cable shield as a guard; the other half, an inverting stage with 10 kΩ in and 390 kΩ of feedback, drives the right leg through 390 kΩ. With the current-feedback input stage, VG runs roughly 0.7 V under the input common-mode voltage; that offset on the guard does no harm in many guarding uses.
notes: RG = 5.6 kΩ gives G = 10.
Supplies are not drawn.

equations.name: Gain, INA128
equations.note: The 50 kΩ is the sum of the two laser-trimmed internal feedback resistors of A1 and A2; their tolerance and drift are inside the gain error and gain drift figures, RG's are not.

where.R1: series resistor from VO to the load

operation.text: A three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier. Two input buffers A1 and A2, each behind an overvoltage protection network, are joined through their 25 kΩ feedback resistors (24.7 kΩ in the INA129) and the external RG; a difference amplifier A3 built with four 40 kΩ resistors subtracts their outputs and refers the result to REF. The input stage uses current feedback, so the bandwidth stays wide at high gain (200 kHz at G = 100).

The die is built in two qualified fabrication flows, named by chip site origin: CSO: SHE and CSO: FRE. Where they differ, the electrical table and the curves give each one. SOIC parts may contain either die; PDIP parts contain CSO: SHE die. Designing to cover both flows is advised.
There is one operating mode. The part works from 4.5 V (±2.25 V) up to 36 V (±18 V) total supply; ±15 V is the supply for best performance. Most parameters change only a little across that range.
Internal protection lets either input sit at up to ±40 V without damage (RS = 0 Ω). Input current against input voltage is plotted in the overvoltage V/I curves.

The linear input range runs from about 2 V above the negative supply to about 2 V below the positive one, but A1 and A2 swing with the differential signal, so the usable common-mode range shrinks as the output grows and as the supply drops; the common-mode range against output voltage curves show it for ±15 V, ±5 V and ±2.5 V. An overload can hide: if both input amplifiers saturate at the same rail, A3 sees almost no difference and the output sits near 0 V even though the inputs are out of range.

The output is measured from REF, normally grounded. REF must be driven from a low impedance: 8 Ω in series with it brings a typical part's CMR down to about 80 dB at G = 1. For single-supply use REF can be lifted to a precise mid-level (for example 2.5 V on 5 V) to centre the output for an ADC; a voltage reference suits, and a resistor divider needs an op amp buffer to avoid hurting CMRR.

One resistor between pins 1 and 8 sets any gain from 1 to 10,000; with nothing connected the gain is 1. The gain resistor table lists exact and nearest 1% values. RG's own tolerance and temperature coefficient add to gain error and drift directly through the gain equation. At high gain RG is small, so wiring resistance matters; sockets add resistance and possibly unstable gain error from about G = 100 upward.
The current-feedback input stage keeps bandwidth wide and settling short at high gain while the supply current stays low.

Offset and drift are laser trimmed, so most designs need no adjustment. Where trimming is wanted, a voltage applied to REF adds to the output; it should come through an op amp buffer so REF stays low impedance and CMR is not lost (see the offset-trim circuit, ±10 mV range).

The inputs are very high impedance (about 10 GΩ) and draw roughly ±2 nA of bias current, which changes little with input voltage. The source must give that current a path to ground; without one the inputs float beyond their common-mode limits and the buffers saturate. With a low differential source resistance one resistor on one input is enough (thermocouple case); with a higher source impedance, two equal resistors keep the input balanced, which can lower offset from bias current and improve high-frequency CMR. A transformer can return the current through a grounded center tap.
Low-frequency noise is about 0.2 µVPP from 0.1 Hz to 10 Hz at G ≥ 100.

Down to ±2.25 V the part performs well, but the internal nodes need headroom, so at low supplies the input common-mode range narrows and the input voltages must be checked against the linear range curves.
Fit a bypass capacitor of 0.1 µF to 1 µF tight against the supply pin and its ground, and add more decoupling between the supply and the part if the supply is noisy or of high impedance.
Put the gain resistor right at pins 1 and 8 to keep that loop small and limit noise pickup. The recommended layout places RG across the top pins and a bypass capacitor next to each supply pin.
